title: Final: a collection from the inside
sub: Budgets, suspension, marking, the plan and cleanup
cards/0/q: A service allocates almost no large objects, yet the trace shows many full collections with reason AllocSmall. How is that possible?
cards/0/options/0: The trigger is the Gen 0 budget, but the GC went deeper: the Gen 2 budget, spent by promoted survivors, was exhausted
cards/0/options/1: AllocSmall means a call to GC.Collect()
cards/0/options/2: Full collections are always labeled AllocSmall
cards/0/options/3: This is how low memory shows up on Linux
cards/0/explain: The reason answers "what triggered it", while the depth is chosen by the budgets of older generations. Many survivors, many promotions, the Gen 2 budget runs out, a full collection, even though the trigger was a small allocation.
cards/1/task: Cache in Gen 2 holds Entry. Make a Gen 0 collection remove Entry while Cache stays alive.
cards/2/q: What is true about suspending threads? Select all.
cards/2/options/0: A thread in a P/Invoke call is in preemptive mode and does not delay the collection
cards/2/options/1: A native call with [SuppressGCTransition] keeps the thread cooperative
cards/2/options/2: A thread in a call-free managed loop is stopped by interruption: such a method is usually fully interruptible
cards/2/options/3: A thread returning from native code during a collection keeps running alongside it
cards/2/options/4: A safepoint is any instruction at which the OS managed to pause the thread
cards/2/explain: Returning from native code checks the flag and waits for the collection to end. A safepoint is only a place where the GC info describes references exactly; the OS can pause a thread anywhere, but that is not yet a safepoint.
cards/3/q: Assemble a whole blocking compacting Gen 0 collection
cards/3/items/0: The Gen 0 budget runs out on the allocation slow path
cards/3/items/2: Mark from roots and marked cards
cards/3/items/3: Plan: plugs, new addresses, the decision to compact
cards/3/explain: Trigger, suspension, marking, plan, rewrite references, copy, release threads. Had the plan decided to sweep, a single sweep would replace the two phases before Restart EE.
cards/4/q: Which line marks a card in the card table, if items has long been in Gen 2?
cards/4/explain: items[3] = fresh writes a reference to a young object into an element of a Gen 2 array: the write barrier marks the card. Writing a number or null needs no barrier, and assignments to local variables do not write into the heap.
cards/5/q: Why does a Gen 0 collection not check whether the Gen 2 object whose card holds the reference is alive?
cards/5/options/0: That would require marking Gen 2, exactly what generations are meant to avoid
cards/5/options/2: The card table also stores whether the object is alive
cards/5/options/3: The write barrier does that check at store time
cards/5/explain: Cards are a conservative approximation: "there may be a reference into a young generation here". The price is that dead Gen 2 objects hold young ones until a full collection.
cards/6/q: Match the situation and what the plan will choose
cards/6/pairs/1/1: The whole region is promoted, no copying
cards/6/pairs/2/0: LOH with no settings and no heap limit
cards/6/pairs/2/1: Sweep: large objects are not moved
cards/7/q: A Span<int> points into the middle of an array. A collection compacted the generation and moved the array. What about the Span?
cards/7/options/0: It is valid: the GC info flags the interior pointer, and the GC shifted it along with the array
cards/7/options/1: The Span now points at the old place; fixed is needed
cards/7/options/2: The array could not move: the Span pins it
cards/7/explain: The GC knows interior pointers on the stack and rewrites them during relocate. Pinning is needed only when the address goes somewhere the GC cannot see it: into native code or a void*.
cards/7/wrong/2: A Span does not pin. The array under it moves freely, and the Span itself is updated.
